title: Newton's laws: force changes motion
summary: A push does not keep a body moving, it changes its velocity. Three laws, one idea, worked on a block and checked on a ramp.

mass.label: $m$
mass.meaning: how much matter resists a change in motion, in kilograms
mass.body: One quantity, two jobs: it resists acceleration in the second law, and it is what gravity pulls on in weight.
mass.example: A 2 kg block is twice as hard to speed up as a 1 kg block.
mass.analogy: How full the shopping trolley is.

force.label: $F$
force.meaning: a push or pull from outside the body, in newtons (N)
force.body: A force is never a property of the body on its own. It comes from somewhere else: a hand, a rope, the ground.
force.example: A hand pushing a block with 6 N.
force.analogy: Somebody else leaning on your trolley.

net.label: $\Sigma F$
net.meaning: every force on the body added as an arrow, the one it actually feels
net.body: Forces are vectors, so direction matters. Two equal forces in opposite directions add to **zero**, and a body with zero net force has zero acceleration.
net.example: 6 N right and 2 N left add to 4 N right.
net.analogy: Two people pushing a door from opposite sides: the door does not move.

accel.label: $a$
accel.meaning: how fast the velocity changes, in m/s²
accel.body: What the second law hands you. Not the speed, but the *rate* at which the speed changes.
accel.example: 3 m/s² means 3 m/s faster every second.
accel.analogy: How quickly the needle on the speedometer climbs.

vel.label: $v$
vel.meaning: speed together with its direction, in m/s
vel.body: Acceleration changes it. A steady force gives a steadily changing velocity, never a constant one.
vel.example: From rest at 3 m/s², after 4 s the block moves at 12 m/s.
vel.analogy: The number the speedometer shows, plus which way you face.

time.label: $t$
time.meaning: how long the force acts, in seconds
time.body: The bridge from acceleration to velocity: starting from rest, $v = at$.
time.example: Three seconds of push give three seconds of speed gain.
time.analogy: How long you keep your foot on the pedal.

weight.label: $W = mg$
weight.meaning: gravity's pull on the mass, about 9.8 N for every kg
weight.body: A force, measured in newtons. On level ground it is cancelled by the normal force, so it usually does not show up in $\Sigma F$.
weight.example: A 2 kg block weighs about 19.6 N.
weight.analogy: The Earth leaning on the trolley, always downward.

normal.label: $N$
normal.meaning: a surface pushing back, perpendicular to itself
normal.body: Not a law of its own: it takes whatever size stops the body sinking into the surface. On level ground $N = mg$; on a ramp at angle $\theta$, $N = mg\cos\theta$.
normal.example: A 30° ramp pushes with about 17 N on a 2 kg block.
normal.analogy: A table that answers exactly as hard as you press on it.

friction.label: $f_k$
friction.meaning: a surface resisting sliding, kinetic friction $f_k = \mu_k N$
friction.body: It opposes sliding, along the surface. It can be zero, and ice is the easy case.
friction.example: With $\mu_k = 0.2$ and $N = 17$ N, friction is about 3.4 N.
friction.analogy: Sandpaper between the trolley and the floor.

first_law.title: Law I: no force, no change
first_law.body: A body keeps its velocity, same speed and same direction, unless a [net:net force] acts on it. Rest is not a special state; it is just the case $v = 0$.
first_law.says: Every body continues in its state of rest, or of uniform motion in a straight line, unless compelled to change that state by forces impressed upon it.
first_law.useWhen: nothing seems to be pushing, and you need to know what the motion does.
first_law.analogy: A puck on ice needs no reason to keep going, only a reason to stop.

second_law.title: Law II: the net force sets the acceleration
second_law.body: $\p{net}{\Sigma F} = \p{mass}{m}\p{accel}{a}$. The net force does not set the velocity, it sets how fast the velocity changes. Double the force and the acceleration doubles; double the mass and it halves.
second_law.says: The change of motion is proportional to the force impressed, and is made in the direction of the straight line in which that force is impressed.
second_law.useWhen: you know the forces and want the motion, or the other way round.
second_law.units: $\Sigma F$ in newtons, $m$ in kilograms, $a$ in m/s².

third_law.title: Law III: forces come in pairs
third_law.body: If A pushes B, then B pushes A with a force of the same size in the opposite direction. The two forces act on **different bodies**, so they never cancel each other out.
third_law.says: To every action there is always an equal and opposite reaction.
third_law.useWhen: you are looking for a force and cannot see where it comes from.
third_law.analogy: Push off a wall on a skateboard and the wall pushes you back.

net_force.title: Net force
net_force.body: Add every force on the body as a vector. Equal and opposite pairs acting on **one** body cancel, but a third-law pair never does, because it is split across two bodies.
net_force.example: A block pulled right with 6 N and left with 2 N has a net force of 4 N to the right.
net_force.useWhen: two forces act in different directions.

weight_vs_mass.title: Mass is not weight
weight_vs_mass.body: [mass:Mass] is a property of the body and is the same everywhere. [weight:Weight] is a force from gravity and does change: on the Moon $g$ is about $1.6$ m/s², so the same mass weighs less.
weight_vs_mass.example: A 2 kg block weighs 19.6 N on Earth and about 3.2 N on the Moon.
weight_vs_mass.useWhen: a problem gives kilograms and asks for a force, or the reverse.

ramp_limit.title: When does a ramp start to slide?
ramp_limit.body: On a ramp, gravity pulls down the slope with $mg\sin\theta$ and friction resists with at most $\mu_s mg\cos\theta$. The mass cancels, so the block starts to slide when $\tan\theta > \mu_s$.
ramp_limit.example: At $\theta = 30°$, $\tan\theta \approx 0.58$, so it slides only if $\mu_s < 0.58$.
ramp_limit.useWhen: you are asked whether a block stays put.

principia.title: Principia, 1687
principia.body: Newton published the three laws in *Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica*. He never wrote $F = ma$: he worked with proportions and geometry, and the equation is later shorthand from Euler.
principia.example: The same book gave the law of gravity, which explained the Moon and the apple with one rule.

sections.title: The one idea
sections.body: Everyday life says a cart stops when you stop pushing, so force must be what **keeps it moving**. Newton's correction is smaller and stranger: a {first_law|body with no net force} keeps its velocity, and a [net:net force] does exactly one thing, it changes [vel:velocity]. That change is [accel:acceleration], and {second_law|the second law} says how much.

sections.title: Three laws, one motion
sections.note: each line is a sentence you can check a situation against

rows.text: A body keeps its velocity unless a [net:net force] acts on it.
rows.note: {first_law|No force, no change}. This is also the definition of an inertial frame.
{second_law|The net force sets the acceleration}, never the velocity.

rows.text: Two bodies always push each other with equal and opposite forces.
rows.note: {third_law|Equal and opposite}, and acting on two different bodies. That is why a rocket works.

sections.title: The problem
sections.body:
A $2$ kg block sits on frictionless ice. A constant [force:push] of $6$ N acts horizontally for [time:$4$ s].

How fast is the block going at the end, and how far has it travelled? Use $g = 9.8$ m/s².

sections.title: Plan
sections.note: three routes; only one uses the right law

routes.title: Route A
routes.why: The push is the only horizontal force, so $\Sigma F$ is known and {second_law|the second law} gives $a$.
routes.whyNot: Nothing. This is the shortest correct route.

routes.title: Route B
routes.why: It looks like the familiar speed formula, and the time is given.
routes.whyNot: The distance is what we are asked to find, so this route assumes its own answer. It also needs an average speed, and the block is speeding up, not cruising.

routes.title: Route C
routes.why: Gravity really does act on the block, so $W$ is a real force.
routes.whyNot: The block is on ice, not falling. Weight and the [normal:normal force] cancel, so they add nothing to $\Sigma F$.

sections.notUsed: Not used: friction. The ice is frictionless, so $f_k = 0$ and the push is the whole net force.

sections.title: Work it through
sections.note: hover a step for its reason and its trap

steps.move: Add the horizontal forces. The [force:push] is the only one.
steps.why: Weight and the normal force are vertical and cancel, and the ice adds no friction. Nothing else touches the block.
steps.whyNot: Do not add the push to the weight: they are perpendicular, so they do not add along one line.

steps.why: {second_law|The second law} defines acceleration as force per unit mass.
steps.whyNot: Do not multiply: a bigger mass is harder to accelerate, so the mass divides.

steps.why: Starting from rest, each second adds $3$ m/s to the velocity.
steps.whyNot: Do not stop at $6/2 = 3$: that is the acceleration, not the velocity.

steps.move: For the distance, the average velocity is $(0 + 12)/2$, and the time is still $4$ s. So $s = \frac{1}{2}at^2$.
steps.why: With constant acceleration the average velocity is halfway between start and end.
steps.whyNot: Do not use $s = \frac{1}{2}vt^2$: the $\frac{1}{2}$ belongs to the acceleration, and $v$ here is the final speed.

sections.title: Put it on a ramp
sections.note: drag the angle and the roughness; the arrows are the pieces of the net force

sections.title: Check yourself
items: A block slides at a steady $2$ m/s on frictionless ice. The net force on it is **zero**, not $2m$.
Doubling the [mass:mass] while keeping the push the same **halves** the [accel:acceleration].
On level ground, weight and the [normal:normal force] cancel, so neither one appears in $\Sigma F$.
A third-law pair acts on **two different bodies**, so the two forces never cancel on one body.
Remove the push and the block does not stop at once: with no friction it keeps its [vel:velocity], as {first_law|the first law} says.

sections.title: Recall
sections.note: answer from memory before you reveal

questions.q: A $4$ kg block starts from rest under a net force of $8$ N. What is its speed after $3$ s?
Which law explains a puck sliding on forever on frictionless ice?
questions.why: No net force means no change in velocity, so it keeps the velocity it has.

questions.q: A ramp is at $\theta = 30°$ and $\mu_s = 0.7$. Does the block start to slide?
options: Only if the block is heavy enough
questions.why: It slides when $\tan\theta > \mu_s$, and {ramp_limit|the mass cancels} out of that comparison.

events.text: Aristotle: motion needs a mover. Carts and arrows in everyday life agree with him.
Galileo: a ball on a smooth, level track keeps rolling. It is the *resistance*, not motion itself, that needs a cause.
Newton, *Principia*: three laws and one universal gravity. {principia|The whole mechanics of the sky in one arrow}.
Today every rocket, brake and satellite is still checked against these three lines.
